speechtext:
During the general election of November, 1965, many university students found themselves disfranchised under the provisions of subsection 9 of section 16 of the Canada Elections Act. speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, April 13, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof-Mr. Hellyer-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext:

DEBATES	April 14, 1967
On clause 2-Canadian forces, Canadian armed forces.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned last night I was in the process of pointing out to the minister that he was flying in the face of convention by trying to unify Canada's armed forces while in the past few years our two traditional allies, the United States and Great Britain, have proceeded to a policy of deunification. I pointed out that at one time Great Britain, Canada and the United States all considered their respective air forces so important that they set them up as separate units. As a matter of fact the United States separated the air force from the army and the navy in 1947.
Toward the end of the sitting yesterday I echoed a question asked by Air Marshal Curtis; "Is the minister out of his mind?" I do not think I am alone in questioning the ability of the minister to make a decision such as the one he made. As a matter of fact I also pointed out last night that the minister found it necessary to fire or retire a great number of high ranking military officers until he found a corps of officers who would agree with the stand he has taken.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
So the minister is sitting on his side of the house stubbornly ignoring all the pleas and suggestions put forward not only by members on this side of the house but also by senior ranking officers who have gone into retirement, either voluntarily or been forced to do it. Even the press of Canada has written about the stubbornness of the minister. As a matter of fact one of Canada's foremost columnists, Mr. Charles Lynch, wrote the following in the Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, March 22:
Mr. Hellyer has locked himself Into so rigid a position in support of the unification bill that it is hard to imagine him accepting major modifications.
We are not asking for major modifications. We are asking for minor, reasonable and sensible modifications to the bill now before us. Mr. Lynch went on to explain the reason the minister will not accept any changes. He wrote the following:
If he did accept them, it is hard to see how he could stomach the political implications of such a humiliation-and that is how his critics would interpret it.
At best, he would have to move to some other portfolio, accepting a major setback to his political ambitions.
April 14, 1967	COMMONS
So it is not only we on this side of the house and some members of the minister's own party who recognize the fact that the minister has political ambitions. It is recognized by all across the country that the minister has designs on the highest office in this land, and in my opinion he is prepared to frustrate the defence efforts of this country in order to further his own political ambitions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Who is Mr. Lynch? He is not a member of parliament.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Lynch says also:
The simplest solution, and the one that most likely would have been adopted had rigor mortis not set in as stiffly as it has, would be to amend the bill in a way that would preserve the army, navy and air force identities within the proposed unified structure.
In other words he suggests integration but not unification. The opinion is now fairly widespread regarding the unacceptability of the concept of unification. As a matter of fact some of the prominent witnesses who appeared before the defence committee were quite convinced that a change in the armed forces to bring about the unification which is now proposed would automatically alter our defence commitments. I should like to quote two or three of these, Mr. Chairman, but I do not want to quote them all because that would be too time consuming. First of all I should like to quote from the evidence of General Charles Foulkes as recorded on page 1220 of the evidence before the defence committee:

However, the roles of these two brigades in NATO are not indicated. Nobody knows what they are going to do-if they do, they do not say so-or under whose auspices these forces will be employed in this world-wide pacification role.
We are suspicious that Canada's defence forces are being tailored for a particular purpose. We suspect that the defence forces are being groomed with the idea in mind of dropping out of our defence commitments in NATO and NORAD and carrying on with only our commitment to the United Nations.
I should like to suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the minister should take a look at history. He would find a very distinct parallel between what is taking place today and what took place prior to the war of 1939-1945. He would find that the attitude of Great Britain and other countries was pacific. At that time the major nations of the world were putting a tremendous amount of faith in the League of Nations. They considered that
National Defence Act Amendment the greatest deterrent to any armed conflict was the world opinion that would be against any kind of war. As a matter of fact, even in the last days before the war the British people were convinced that the public opinion that would be aroused against any action taken by Adolf Hitler would force him to recant and proceed with his plans in a peaceful manner.
We find ourselves in the same situation today, Mr. Chairman. We have people advocating that we ignore what is commonly called power politics and pin our hopes entirely on the United Nations. As a matter of fact the Prime Minister of this country, before he was prime minister, made a speech at the University of British Columbia on this thought that public opinion would deter any future war. He was speaking to the University of British Columbia on the transformation of the traditional concept of international power politics to the rule by international law, international organization and international force. He had this to say in 1961:
During this period of transformation, it is certain that force will continue to be a basis of policy. In the past, it has often been used with cruel injustice. But not always. In the hands of conscientious patrons it has also been the instrument for maintaining rough international justice, as well as security and stability. It is when great power is controlled by governments that cannot be counted on to use it justly or responsibly, that we grow fearful. So we collect counterforce and use it through power politics to prevent ourselves being overpowered. If we did not, diplomacy and the negotiation of disputes would be determined by the threat of one sided force in the background.
This, then, is the situation which in reality determines our approach to the ideal disarmament and the abolition of national force. All our high sounding declarations must be interpreted in that context. We should not try to deceive ourselves.
Well now, Mr. Chairman, this was the attitude of the present Prime Minister of this country. He said, and I repeat:
This, then, is the situation which in reality determines our approach to the ideal disarmament and the abolition of national force. All our high sounding declarations must be interpreted in that context.
How does this statement fit into the present situation? We find that the Minister of National Defence is trying to abolish the traditional fighting forces of this country. We find the Secretary of State for External Affairs trying to assure this house that we are not going to change any of our international commitments. When he was referring to NATO and NORAD he made it very plain to this house that the government had no intention of changing those commitments for the moment. There was no suggestion we would carry on these commitments for a year or five
14922	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment years or ten years; he said "For the moment".
I think we are entitled, and the people of Canada are entitled, to know that these commitments will be continued for an indefinite period.
As we all know, the NORAD agreement will be renegotiated next year. The question I should like to ask is this. Will our defence forces be changed to such an extent that we will not be capable of being a partner in NORAD? Is this a deliberate move by the government of this country to develop forces capable only of action in respect to our commitments to the United Nations? The attitude of the Prime Minister leads one to believe that he is staking his political future on the hope that moral suasion will be an effective deterrent to war. If it is, it will be the first time in history that this has happened.
It might be pointed out that the only countries that have really followed the dictates of the United Nations have been the western countries. The eastern countries, for example Soviet Russia, have used the veto over 100 times. The only large concessions that have been made have come from the western countries. In spite of this the Prime Minister of this country, according to his speech to the University of British Columbia in 1961, believes that the United Nations can mobilize the moral forces of the international community against any bloc which threatens world peace. I remind you that the same thing was said of the League of Nations before the war of 1939.
Referring again to the speech delivered by the Prime Minister I find this:
The United Nations assembly is creating something in the nature of a world public opinion. This does have an effect in checking, if not yet in preventing, aggressive actions by predatory individual states. It has its own power for peace.
Lord help us, Mr. Chairman, if we rely strictly on world public opinion for the peace of this country. I say I suspect the change in the military forces of this country and the adoption of an untried method of operation is directly designed to tailor the forces of this country for the United Nations, and for the withdrawal of this country from its commitments to NORAD and NATO.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
I am not alone in that thought. Lieutenant General Moncel, when questioned about changes in commitments, said this at page 1305 of the committee evidence:
-if you do change your commitments and produce a unified force to meet these much reduced

commitments, then you should bear in mind that you are never again going to have a commitment that might call for something other than a unified force.
Lieutenant General Moncel was saying that once a force is unified it can only be used in the context where a unified force is necessary, and it will not be useful for NATO or NORAD. Air Vice Marshal Hendrick at page 1451 of the committee evidence agreed with Lieutenant General Moncel and said:

This seems to be inevitable from the events that are taking place and the equipment policies that are going on.
It is all very well for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to say that we do not intend to change our commitments for the moment. We want to know, are the defence forces of this country being tailored to suit United Nations projects to the exclusion of commitments that we have with NATO and NORAD? Lieutenant General Moncel has suggested that this is so. He said that once you start down the road of unification there is no turning back.
Members of this house and the people of this country have a right to demand a fuller explanation from the ministers than has been given up to the present time. I suggest that consideration should be given to withdrawing this bill, and more thought should be given to the commitments we have abroad.

Mr. Chairman, for reasons that will be obvious in a moment or two, I do not rise to discuss the terms of the bill now before us. Neither do I intend to make any comment on the nature of the debate or on the positions taken by the opposing sides. But I do have a suggestion to make regarding our procedure. I make it in the best of faith, and I make it now in the hope that it might be considered over the week end or perhaps for even a day or two longer than that.
April 14, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment
If I may say so without arousing any feelings, it is now fairly clear that there will be a time established when this debate will come to an end. That may be arrived at by agreement or it may be arrived at by the procedures laid down in one of the provisional rules under which we are operating. At the moment I am not discussing the rights or wrongs of that course. I am simply suggesting that it is fairly obvious that a time limit will be set.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it is a matter of some concern that during the time this bill is before us we should have discussion on a number of its clauses. It looks to me as though the earliest this debate could end under provisional standing order 15-A would be a week from next Tuesday, but I think it would be most unfortunate if all our time between now and then were spent on clause 2. That may happen, though there is always the possibility that the debate on clause 2 could end even without any arrangement or understanding.
But, Mr. Chairman, there are 65 clauses in the bill and two schedules. I recognize that many of them that are clauses which contain details may not need to be discussed at length, but there are some very important provisions in some of the other clauses and I think we ought to have a chance to discuss them. It would be most unfortunate if the application of rule 15-A were such that we spent all our time on clause 2 and then had to vote on all the other clauses without any discussion. This would be unfortunate in terms of the bill and unfortunate for parliament, and I can readily imagine the things that will be said if this happens. All this could be avoided if we could come to an agreement.
I am not proposing that anything should be done in any other way than by agreement. Let me put it this way. Maybe on Monday night we could agree to adjourn the debate on clause 2 and proceed to take up some of the other clauses. I am not suggesting that a vote be taken on clause 2 at that time. I am only suggesting that we adjourn the debate on it and move on to some of the other clauses which deserve to be discussed. I understand that clause 6 should be discussed at some length and a few other clauses dealing with uniforms and rank structures in the services. There are also matters in the schedules that should be discussed.
It may be argued that we should not discuss these other matters until we have decided on the principle of a unified force which is
[Mr. Knowles.J

set out in clause 2, but I suggest we should not try to reach a decision on that clause by forcing a vote on it if hon. members want to discuss other clauses. Let us not get ourselves into a position where we can be called upon to make a final decision on a bill 64 clauses of which have not been discussed at all.
Again I say I am not assessing blame. I am not saying the opposition is preventing the discussion of the other clauses by discussing clause 2, and I am not suggesting the government is to blame for asking the house to consider the use of standing order 15-A. I am asking all of us to face the fact that we have a limited amount of time left-it might be seven or eight days or it might be longer-to discuss all the clauses in the bill which hon. members want to discuss. I am sure there are many other clauses that are important, and they should get a bit of an airing in the committee of the whole.
Of course I hope the application of standing order 15-A will not be too severe. As I say, even the minimum times allowed under it would keep this debate going in committee stage and on third reading until a week from Tuesday night, but it may extend longer than that. All I am asking is that we think about this over the week end and come to some agreement.
I have looked up the rules and I believe you would have difficulty, Mr. Chairman, if a motion were made to stand clause 2 without general agreement. There would be no point in having a procedural wrangle over that. But I think we could have an understanding that having spent 10 or 11 days on clause 2, without taking the vote on it at this point, we should go on to discuss the other clauses. The result of this might be that if members of the official opposition continue to stage their case on some of the other clauses they would persuade the government that the bill should be held off. This question was raised in the standing committee on national defence and the Judge Advocate General pointed out that there are certain regulations which cannot be completed until the form of the bill is known. Let me give an example. The committee already has proposed an amendment which gives to the governor in council the responsibility to designate the names of the ranks to be used, whereas in the original draft of the bill this power was given to the minister. This means there will be a difference in the type of order which must be promulgated in order to give practical effect to this provision.
It is quite impossible for the legal staff to properly prepare the orders until they know what actually is the text of the law. The Judge Advocate General said it would be several months after the bill has been approved by parliament before we would be in a position to ask the governor in council to proclaim it.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: On that point may I say that I fail to see what effect the fact that orders will have to be issued down through the services will have on the matter of proclamation. This will in no way be affected by the fact that the bill has been passed by parliament but is unproclaimed. The proclamation of the bill in the end will not take away the uncertainty. Certainly any problems which might exist in respect of the issuing of orders down through the various services cannot have any effect on the proclamation. The bill will not be changed in any shape or form, nor will any new wording be introduced in the bill. After the bill is passed, if it is passed, there will be no changes made in the bill itself. The final proclamation of the bill will give it full effect and force under the law. If the proclamation is held up I think this will leave in the minds of the people a doubt concerning what the minister intends to do.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE

My hon. friend seems to miss the point. A number of changes were made to the text of the law during the hearings of the committee on national defence, and these


changes have been recommended to the House of Commons and this committee. It is possible that during the course of the deliberations in this committee there might be other amendments. I cannot say whether there will or will not be. It is quite possible, however, that we might find that other technical changes are desirable in the interests of implementing the general proposal. If that should happen this would alter the regulations which must be prepared based on the law. Consequently I believe it is a perfectly valid proposition that the staff cannot provide the draft regulations until they know precisely what the law looks like.

Far from my missing the point, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that what the minister has just said of course bears out exactly what I have put forward. Nothing in this bill can be changed in any way, shape or form after it has been passed by this house. Any amendments which may be put forward by the government or accepted by the government as proposed by the opposition cannot be made after the bill has passed this house. These changes must be made during our clause by clause consideration. I suggest the regulations will be made in accordance with the bill as passed.
The suggestion that proclamation be withheld leaves me uneasy in my mind. I have an underlying uneasiness that the minister proposes to hold up proclamation because he is finally afraid to implement the purposes of this bill. Maybe he has received some advice from the cabinet that we should not go ahead with these measures, in which case we are now wasting our time. We should know now that when this bill is passed it will go immediately to that other place, where I hope it will be given long, serious and sober thought. Perhaps they will throw it out.
We should have proclamation at the earliest possible time following passage of the bill. We do not want any hidden idea that the minister is getting advice from down the line somewhere regarding possible changes. Regulations can only be made according to the bill as passed by this house, and the bill as passed by this house will be the bill finally proclaimed. Why should we wait for months?
I read over General Allard's evidence, and assure you that he said it would take some time before the bill would be proclaimed and that when he was good and ready he would tell the minister to proclaim it. That is in the evidence and I heard him say it. I wondered
April 14, 1967

about it at the time. It seems to me that withholding proclamation after passing the bill for any purpose whatever will raise the speculation that something else will be slipped in, in some way or another.
I am very clear as to what the minister has said, but surely we cannot hold off proclamation after passing the bill. To do so would be completely and utterly wrong and would leave a feeling in the minds of all members of the house that there is something devious going on. The minister gave one example of why proclamation could be withheld, but surely that related merely to a departmental matter. How can they go ahead and implement these measures if the bill is not promulgated? These people know it will be promulgated unless the government is defeated in the meantime. That might change the whole pattern.
In any event the armed forces will be left in doubt about the whole matter until proclamation. Whether that takes four months or four years does not make much difference if these measures are to be implemented on a piecemeal basis, but this will leave an uneasiness in the minds of many people, and this uneasiness will find its way to service personnel. This in turn will have an effect on the morale of our servicemen. Surely the minister must realize that.

I have not spoken so far on this bill although I have intended to do so for some months. So far as I am personally concerned this is the time to speak. Whether the proposal suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should be considered over the week end-and
National Defence Act Amendment that is another matter-it is at this time I feel I should speak on the bill. If the hon. member's proposal was accepted we would to a certain extent be anticipating the prerogative of Mr. Speaker to allow two days for the proposal of amendments under the new procedures, but I think the suggestion is worthy of consideration.
Many hon. members have said they had not intended to speak during this debate but have done so because of the arrogance of the minister and the lack of information. I have always felt that the part of this bill which abolishes the navy is shocking. For many months I have felt that I must say something in this regard. The traditions and the separate identity of the navy are very important. On many occasions I have risen in my place and said that I for one have been alarmed at the lack of attention given to the sea and its importance to this country which perhaps has the longest coast line in the world. This is a nation of landlubbers. Instead of being proud of the traditions of the sea and bringing up our young people accordingly, we forget about it.
By passing this bill we will completely wipe out the navy. That is a retrograde step, and as one who has been kicking around the waterfront for many years, and who was privileged to sail from the rugged shores of Canada and safely return, I am alarmed. I think this step will set us back many years.
The tradition of the navy is very interesting. I wonder what will happen to all those posters that one recalls in a nostalgic way which suggested to our youth "Join the navy and see the world"? I suppose the old slogan that a sailor has a girl in every port will no longer be of any value. I do not know what the girls will do or whether they are concerned, but that has always been part of the adventure of joining the navy. That idea will be completely forgotten as part of our Canadian way of life. I have very carefully read the testimony and the speeches pertaining to the navy, and I find they have been mostly one-sided. No answers were given in respect of the pride of separate identity. Our youth will no longer have the opportunity of feeling that pride.
If one needed an excuse to take part in this debate the intervention by the Minister of Transport last Friday is excuse enough. The hon. member for Grenville-Dundas has referred to one or two quotations from the speech of the Minister of Transport. I am comforted by the fact that in her excellent
14930	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment address she used them to even greater advantage than I might have done, Mr. Chairman. I was amazed to sit in my place and listen to the Minister of Transport refer, as he always does, to what went on in the minds of the members of the cabinet and other members on the government side regarding this abolition bill. Why a minister from Newfoundland should speak in such gloating terms about doing away with the navy is beyond my comprehension. Perhaps that is the reason he was sent up north this week.
The minister has had many troubles in his department with respect to navigation on the St. Lawrence. The Registrar General was in the chamber a moment ago following the debate. I would have liked to hear him express his opinions on this matter. We all know the reason for not having Canadian navigation on the St. Lawrence river. It is because we do not have qualified seamen here. Seamen of this type are not trained in Canada. We have to go to the United Kingdom for most of our pilots. Our young fellows do not follow the sea.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Many measures have been taken by the Department of Transport to try to interest our youth in this career. We have a coast guard training school. Its members are in naval uniform. We are trying to build up a pride of service there. If this bill goes through where will Canada stand as far as our navy is concerned? We will have coast guard officers and ferry boat captains. Won't that be nice when we meet the nations of the world at naval meetings? I recall nostalgically the large convoy meetings that were held in Halifax and Norfolk during the last war, when the various ships and navies came into port. It was a sight to see them all in their naval uniforms receiving orders for the convoys that were the lifeblood of the troops and the people in Europe. Will it not be ridiculous if we have another war and hundreds of naval officers are gathered in a room planning the convoys and the Canadians are sitting there in their jolly green jumpers? It is too ridiculous, in my opinion, to even talk about.
The remarks of hon. members opposite, and particularly those of the Minister of Transport, show what little consideration was given in cabinet to this matter. I searched the record vainly for answers to the questions we have asked. I searched for answers to the questions we have raised about naval tradition, particularly in the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), a distinguished naval officer. We have asked why morale is

DEBATES	April 14, 1967
reduced, recruiting so difficult, and our young people are leaving the service. The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) and the Minister of Transport dragged in everything they could about the swingers, Marshall McLuhan and other things.
I have mentioned the naval record of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), and I wish to pay tribute to the admirals who courageously came forward and were criticized by many hon. members for stating their opinions. I have read the testimony of Admirals Lan-dymore and Rayner. Everybody in Canada, regardless of the outcome of this debate, owes them a debt of gratitude for putting their case forward.

speechtext:
I pay tribute to these admirals for expressing their views in a straightforward way. I have looked through the record of this debate for answers from the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), the chairman of the committee, the Minister of Transport and others who have spoken on that side of the house, to the questions that have been raised. One remark by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) struck me as needing further explanation, though I appreciate that he did not put it forward in too serious a way. He said that if the navy on the east coast was not able to do the job, then the west coast could take over. This burns me up. There are many good sailors on the east and west coasts and they were interchangeable during the war, but Halifax was the only city in Canada that really felt the brunt of the war. Those in Halifax knew the battle of the Atlantic. They knew what it was to lose sons, fathers and brothers.
April 14, 1967	COMMONS
1 can pay tribute to Halifax because I am not from that city. We in Saint John rival Halifax, but that was the only Canadian city to really feel the effects of the war. I think this is why tradition dies hard down there, and we should take note of their feelings in this matter. I say to the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) that the people in this area have experienced the hardships of war and we should pay attention to their feelings. Not only will they be hard hit when the navy is abolished, but it will cut into their whole way of life and decrease to a sad extent the interest of those who go to sea.
I wish to make a personal remark here because many of us who were in the services during the second world war-I do not believe for one minute in trading war records-did not end up doing the jobs we wanted to do. The second world war was very different from the first in this respect. In the second world war we dreamed of being Spitfire pilots and leading commando raids, but this was not possible for all of us. This was the situation of about 90 per cent of those who served in the second world war. In the first world war you fought in trenches, and that was it; it was simple. You might not have lasted long, but there it was.
The second world war was global. We had different responsibilities, and many of us were frustrated by what we were doing and were perhaps not happy about it. I for one have always felt that although many Canadians made just as great a contribution as anyone else, they would have been happier with a little more glory and glamour. It could be the case that the minister, in becoming mixed up in this business, is carrying over a frustration from some of the things that did not turn out the way he wanted in so far as his own personal career was concerned; and I say that without any animosity.
I have read the record of this debate to try to find the reason behind this proposal. I have tried to find where the unification idea came from. The other day somebody told me that when he was at a defence college they used to throw this out as an exercise when you first arrived. They said "Go and write an article on unification", as though it was a big joke and something very hypothetical. Is this where it came from? Did some junior officer at defence college write a thesis on unification, and was it picked up? Did the idea come from this unknown wing commander who hovers around this chamber on cloud nine? Who conceived this idea? We do not know where it came from.
National Defence Act Amendment
We have not even heard from anybody who supports it. There must be some retired officer in this country who could come forward and support it. I have looked for such support and for the answers to the questions we have raised. I have looked to the navy for support for this proposal. I read the debate on the contention put forward by Admiral Rayner, and I compliment him for putting it forward. I was amazed to find this answer given by Admiral Rayner, as reported at page 2022 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 31 of the committee, and I presume it is true because it was not challenged. This is an insight into the thinking of the minister:

I think the uncertainty is caused in large measure by changes in plans. To give you an example of what I mean, in the spring of 1964-in April-the Minister of National Defence went to Esquimau and talked to the sailors there. He was questioned on interchangeability.
He explained that he did not see why an army cook could not cook just as well at sea as he could ashore; and similarly, with a radar technician, he did not see why any air force radar technician could not serve just as well at sea in a ship as he could on an R.C.A.F. station.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Everyone knows that a cook aboard a ship is important when sailors have to be at sea for three months or more. I admit that one could recruit a cook from the shore and put him on a ship, but he would not last very long, and that is why cooks have been dumped overboard late at night. Another question was put to Admiral Rayner concerning the uniform. In answer he quoted the minister as follows:
Well, take the case of the Bonaventure, for example. When you have soldiers and airmen and sailors all on the Bonaventure and have them all falling in in these different uniforms-
Does the minister mean he is going to put the three services on the decks of the Bonaventure, if we ever do get the bloody ship fixed, and have them running around there? What is going on in the mind of the minister is fantastic. I suppose this is the reason he wants the three services in the same uniform.
The navy is a very special service. It is a service which demands high quality and high standards. It is the one above other services which has a definite role to play. Yet the navy is the first to get the axe. Those of us who went to sea-and I for one have never felt that the sea got me-have recognized that one must have special attributes to join the navy.
14932	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment
Admiral Landymore, in his brief on the navy's place in unification dated February 1966, pointed out in admirable fashion that, first of all, a young man going to sea must be a tradesman as well as a sailor. I do not know which qualification he puts first; they are interchangeable. A sailor has one particular job to do aboard a ship, but he has to learn many other duties. I know this is why we have had difficulties in building up a merchant navy in Canada. We are a very affluent country and our sailors are reluctant to undertake the hardships at sea without receiving wages comparable to those of their fellow workers on land. This makes it more difficult to interest men in a merchant seaman's career.
Admiral Landymore in his brief remarked on the extra hardships imposed on sailors because of their long absences from home. In this regard they are unlike other members of the service. This is particularly true in peacetime when they are away from their families, and that is an important point in today's modern society. Sometimes they are away for long periods of time. For this reason among others there is a lower re-engagement rate for those in the navy. The navy has a hard time to hold them in the service.
The third point Admiral Landymore made, and which I think is of great significance, refers to the separate identity and esprit de corps which are particularly necessary aboard a ship. The best sailors are those who possess this spirit. The same applies to a football team, and we dress a football team in a special uniform so as to build up the necessary esprit de corps. The leaders of the teams are those who have the most spirit and who take the teams and their colours seriously. Yet it is the best men, the ones who want the traditions of the silent service to be maintained, who will be the first to go under the plan proposed by the minister. They will be disappointed and will leave the service.
On page 4 of his brief Admiral Landymore said:
The man we want is one who under no circumstances will let his ship down, who is proud of his uniform, who does his job to the best of his ability regardless of how long it takes him to do it, and who is ready to die if need be, to prove he is better than his enemies.
In closing I ask again the question, who is the power behind this unification program? Where did the idea come from? Did it come from the unknown wing commander? What is his experience? We know the experience of the minister and I have suggested, I hope not

DEBATES	April 14, 1967
unfairly, that perhaps what motivated the minister was a touch of frustration during the second world war. Is the minister saying that he and this unknown wing commander have more knowledge than the 80 officers who were retired or have resigned? This is the conclusion one must reach. We did not hear an answer from the Minister of Transport, nor did we hear an answer from the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), however distinguished a war record he may have.
My final plea is to ask the minister not to rush this program of unification. The minister was in the house, as I was, when the defence production bill was being debated. I am not harking back to the pipe line issue, which is another story, but the minister will recall the defence production legislation brought forward by the late Mr. Howe, who asked for blanket authority. Some of us took an interest in this, particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Why did Mr. St. Laurent, the prime minister of the day, send the late Mr. Howe on a fishing trip during which time he changed some of the key clauses in the bill?
This might be a way out; but no, this is an action of an arrogant government. Introducing a common uniform will not bring about an economy. There is no rhyme nor reason in the loss of identity of the services. I like the comparison of this government with its prime minister to a crew, adrift 40 miles out at sea, and the prime minister saying "Untie the ship". I think this is an excellent naval example describing what is happening here.

April 14, 1967	COMMONS
I have a copy of a telegram sent to the Prime Minister by the Naval Officers Association of New Brunswick and I should like to read it into the record:
The Naval Officers Association of New Brunswick at annual meeting in Saint John April 7, 1967 unanimously agree that while we wholeheartedly approve of integration at the command level, for logistic support, in administration and of medical services, we abhor the thought of total unification of the armed forces.
We feel that the arguments put forward opposing unification as expressed before the House of Commons defence committee far outweigh the ideals as put forward by the defence minister. We concur and fully endorse the recent statement of Lord Louis Mountbatten and urgently request you and your ministers to take appropriate steps to ensure that the three services retain their individual identities which we sincerely believe is vitally essential to the morale of our armed forces.
Naval Officers Association of New Brunswick
This telegram speaks for itself, Mr. Chairman. I hope the minister will take note of this telegram from men who probably know a lot more about this problem than the minister and I. I have made my plea and I hope the minister will take full cognizance of it. He has made exceptions already in the case of the Scottish regiments which can retain their kilts and in the case of the French through his offer to retain the Royal 22nd Regiment.

I am intervening in the debate for the same reason but because of the arrogance of the members of the opposition. They are doing their utmost to delay the passage of this bill, and that is my reason for taking part in the debate.
National Defence Act Amendment [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, as Canada is becoming increasingly aware of the role it can play on the international scene, it will be able to perform that role even more effectively.
Indeed, our country is undergoing deep changes at present and thanks to its dynamism and its vitality, it is now reflecting in foreign countries a favourable and influential image.
Canadians are proud to note the increasingly important position their country is occupying within the United Nations, and they are also proud when they realize that Canada is providing developing countries not only with financial assistance, but also all kinds of assistance in every field, with the help of its experts, which gives our country a sense of leadership and dynamism.
Bill No. C-243, which we are still studying today, deals with the proposed unification of the Canadian armed forces. Therefore, this intention on the part of Canada is no secret. Some people, afraid of the decision we are about to make in this respect, are fighting it desperately. They are against the new plan. However, I must tell them that a number of experts in this field have pointed out to us in various ways the importance of unification and of certain legislative and national values implied in the concept.
I should like to make some comments on Personnel and Careers in the Canadian armed forces. First of all, I should like to read a statement made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) in answer to certain assertions made by some of the witnesses who appeared before the committee on national defence. They claimed that integration and unification would turn the members of our armed forces into jacks of all trades. Then on December 7, 1966 the minister said:
The combat units will retain their identity, and their specialized functions and training. It is important to state-
-continues the Minister of National Defence-
-that it is not and never has been any part of the planning associated with unification to convert our servicemen to "jacks-of-all-trades". An infantry soldier will not be asked to do the job of a sailor in a fighting ship; a sailor will not be asked to fight in an infantry platoon; and a fighter pilot will not be required to drive a tank.
I agree with the minister whole-heartedly. Besides, is it not true that those who put this argument forward seem to ignore the following fact: All the members of a defence force
14934	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment must acquire a certain basic training and discipline, although each service must play its proper role.
I must also point out that, in considering this matter more closely, I based my opinion on the very evidence given by qualified people responsible for setting up and carrying out the said Personnel and Careers plan. It is all there in black and white and references are available for those who might have some doubts.
As announced last fall, the major interest of career men as far as prospective promotions are concerned is based on the new structures. These measures, however, constitute a serious problem in the sense that they bring about the dearth of subjects, that is, there were 346 subjects and there are now only 97. The chief of personnel, Air Marshal Reyno testifying before the national defence committee on February 9 said as reported on page 597 of the proceedings:
I should add that this reduction has been achieved with remarkably few complaints, and no loss of efficiency, and will in time produce considerable economy through consolidation of training.
The many trades involving few people have been merged into 97 trades involving larger numbers. The restrictive rank structure of the smaller group has been eliminated by the personnel concerned having the opportunity to compete for promotion in the larger group. In doing this we have eliminated a number of minor trades which were unattractive as career prospects.
Mr. Chairman, this is the opinion of an expert who is currently member of the general staff and who would be responsible for the success of integration and unification.
This new structure required an increase of 14 per cent in pay and this has been the starting point of the first revision in pay in 20 years. And it is that review, postponed for such a long time, which undoubtedly put the positions of the members of the armed forces on the same level as civilian positions in industry. Of course, that was only the beginning of the readjustment. Several other things, beneficial to servicemen's families, as, for instance, certain allowances, etc. clearly indicate all the efforts made to protect the rights of these people and their families. Some persons asserted that all those steps could have been taken without resorting to unification. But I should like to point out that the program is still incomplete. It cannot be denied that it was that reorganization which revealed all those shortcomings and it was that progressive spirit, put in concrete form

DEBATES	April 14, 1967
by unification, which brought forth the solution of those difficulties which were due to incompleteness.
After reading once again Marshal Reyno's brief, we notice that he deals accurately with the conditions and qualifications necessary to have armed forces made up of men interested in a promising career. And he sees in them individuals able to adjust to new conditions.
Moreover, that reorganization attracts individuals able to adjust to these new conditions. Reclassification will add to the flexibility of the personnel. It will be an organization able to compete with industry in the matter of manpower, because its leaders will be able to initiate its members in various jobs so that they in turn, can become leaders, able to take over.
We can but approve the tremendous amount of work that has been done and applied by the new organization.
Air Marshal Reyno summarized his testimony by saying, as reported on page 605 of proceedings No 16, justifying every opinion expressed before the national defence committee-and this confirms that those responsible for carrying out unification are aware of their problems-
Finally, I would like to say that we are extremely conscious that personnel constitute our single greatest asset and that is worth repeating and also that we would fail in our task if we did not ensure that the complete management system would respond to the needs of the commanders as users of the manpower in both peace and war.
I would point out again that the development of our structure and the management organization is the result of continuous consultation with our field commanders and senior managers and I am confident that the system I have outlined will meet the requirement.
Mr. Chairman, if I quote some sentences, some excerpts from our experts currently responsible for the application of such integration and unification, it is to counterbalance, as I said at the beginning, the other outside experts who claim that unification and integration will not bring about the hoped for results.
If we understand the main objective of the personnel and careers program within a unified defence force, we must recognize, in view of the overall plan, that we can no longer delay unification which will achieve good results, both economically and administratively. I am sure that those who oppose it, for patriotic reasons which must, however, be admired, will adapt themselves and will substitute to the traditional customs the necessities of the role Canada must play in the council of nations.
April 14, 1987	COMMONS
Even Air Marshal Sharp, vice commander of defence command, favours the new organization of the personnel and careers program. In his evidence before the defence committee, he singled out seven reasons which justify the move. Those reasons can be found on page 460 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence for February 7, 1967, and here is the table set up by Mr. Sharp:
1.	An occupation which is clearly worthwhile.
2.	Work which challenges the capabilities of the individual.
3.	Work which employs up-to-date methods and equipment.
4.	Work in an atmosphere or environment which accepts the change necessary to keep up with advances in science: an environment which is recognized as a leader in the field.
5.	Advancement based on ability, and at a reasonable rate.
6.	Reasonable financial and other compensations.
7.	Recognition by the public and friends that the individual's work is demanding.
And, by the way to prove the measure of success which was achieved, he added:
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Full implementation of the policy contained in the white paper will go a long way to providing these necessary conditions.
The important thing in considering this matter, and 1 hope everyone has now realized it, is that there is no question at all of turning members of the armed forces into jacks of all trades, as was suggested by some witnesses before the committee. I mentioned the fact at the beginning of my remarks when I referred to this statement of the minister in his speech to the house on December 7 last. I am also gratified to note that staff officers have repeated this assurance during the sittings of the defence committee.
I am positive, Mr. Chairman, that we have recognized, up to now, that any person who joins the armed forces has great and new opportunities to make quite a promising career. Those same recruits will have the advantage, with that new organization, to go ahead in a force which will facilitate their promotion according to their ability and their potential and not simply on seniority. The military candidate has a greater realization of the special interest taken by the Department of National Defence in his possibilities and his welfare, contrary to what some have attempted to make us believe. In fact, that interest has already been shown by the new structures, a salary increase, an allowance increase and the undertaking of a planned career. Therefore, he will rightly be proud to represent Canada when putting on the new
National Defence Act Amendment proposed uniform and he will be happy to wear it.
The integration and unification project is not new; for many years, prominent people, civilians as well as military men, have considered it. Within the Canadian forces, and even at the Liberal national convention in January 1958, when the Liberal party was in opposition, the project was revived and this can be seen from the minutes of that convention as shown on page 223 of the proceedings.
Since the coming into power of the Liberal party in 1963, it has been the first task to which the Minister of National Defence has set himself. As early as March 1964, the white paper on defence was published and since then integration has been emphasized, the unification stage being the next problem which the defence staff will tackle.
Since the publication of that white paper, that is three years ago, the matter has been constantly raised in the House of Commons and it has made the headlines not only in the press, but also on television and radio. Finally, all sources of information have stopped reporting the views of experts and so-called experts on the matter.
For the past three years, the standing committee on defence has been sitting and hearing witnesses, not to mention that certain politicians kept debating the matter and that the news media did not fail to talk about it.
We can very frankly say that the opponents of the principle of the bill were given ample opportunities to present their views.
The defence committee, which sat from February 7 until March 21, held 55 meetings and heard more than 30 witnesses. As a member of this committee, I can tell the members of this house that the same questions were duly put to each witness. In short, I believe that we have debated this subject long enough for the past three years, that the house has now reached the last stage of discussion on this bill, and that the opposition would be acting in bad faith if it attempted once again to make the headlines as we have known it to do during the flag debate.
In all that time, opposition members have had the privilege, and they used it, to criticize the project. You will agree with me that, in three years, everything that could be said was said long ago. But there is a constant repetition of what has already been said.
As a party in opposition, they have done their duty to the people, and therefore a decision must be made. Whether they accept the
14936	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment principle or vote against the legislation is their privilege. They must go one way or the other, and not indulge in endless debate.
I fully realize, Mr. Chairman, that I am not an expert on military matters and yet, as I read the proceedings of the defence committee-of which I am a member-what struck me was the appropriateness of the action taken for the realization and success of the amalgamation of our three armed forces into a single Canadian force.
If we want to define the word "unification" and make its meaning known, I wonder why we are taking so long to reach a decision on that matter. Let us think of the very aim of that meaning and we have in fact unification. That very meaning of the combat forces differs not in their aims and objectives but rather because of their means and tactics, in short because of their instruments.
Moreover, in view of the vastness of the country in which the three defence services operate, would not unification help to smooth out the difficulties which arise due to the lack of communications between headquarters and the field services?
Other countries, which are not faced with such a widespread territory, have not felt the same problem. After weighting all the points raised here, I think that a decision must be reached for unification.
Before concluding my observations, Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to quote, in summary, the concept of the commander in chief of the Canadian forces, General Allard, at the end of his brief submitted to the committee on national defence. Here is the opinion of the commander in chief of the Canadian forces, whose task it will be to bring into being such a unification, in which he believes whole-heartedly, as can be seen on page 1770 of the minutes and proceedings No. 27. Here is what he said, and I quote:
In summary, then, gentlemen, the situation is this: The idea of a single force, in a single, distinctively Canadian uniform, working, living, training, and- most important-thinking together as one entity is an exciting and challenging idea. After all it is designed to meet the problems of a modern world -a scientific world-which is growing away beyond the barriers of the past at a speed that cannot stand the slow pace of yesterday. For all this, you know that we do not intend to proceed in haste-
I said it was a starting point-but rather in a carefully planned manner which will extend over a number of years. All that is required now is the authority to do so.
Mr. Chairman, before resuming my seat, I appeal for the last time to the hon. members opposing Bill No. C-243 to grant the general,

Mr. Chairman, I believe it is customary for anybody embarking on a discussion of matters military to try to establish his credentials. In my case I have none. I am certainly a layman, not an expert. However, I confess that as a civilian I volunteered my services to the army and served therein, volunteered my services to the R.C.A.F. and served therein, and got out as fast as I could when the war was over. I have served in the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Royal Air Force, and under an American general, British officers and Canadian officers. I believe my experiences with senior officers have been the same as 99 per cent of the troops -most unhappy ones. Like many serving personnel I could never tell for certain whether I was going to be courtmartialled or praised. So with this limited background I have naturally refrained from debating this subject.
On the other hand, it is true that I did serve in a theatre of war where it was very hard to distinguish the services. Even though I was nominally in the Royal Canadian Air Force, at the time I wore a green uniform in the jungles of Burma I found it was just as smelly, dirty and dilapidated looking as the battledress I wore in the army and the dress uniform I sometimes wore in the air force. I do not think that is the key issue, and if I pose today as one giving advice to the minister it is as one who is trying to find an answer from the point of view of a layman trying to make the right decision.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
This bill has a finality about it that makes it imperative that we give it more than the casual type of attention that we give to bills that can be amended from year to year as more experience is gained. I have been watching this debate. I think the position of the people of Canada was well put last autumn in a Globe and Mail editorial dated November 7 which said:
There must be a most thorough public discussion of where the Canadian forces reorganization act is leading us. Mr. Hellyer must be made to show the urgent and valid reasons for undertaking the changes he has proposed or forced to admit that there are none.
April 14, 1967	COMMONS
That puts the matter into a simple sentence. Has this information been made available to the House of Commons and to the public?
One of the subjects that was debated at length in the defence committee and the committee of the whole was the morale of the armed forces. Was recruiting falling off, was recruiting holding steady? I have looked at the evidence on both sides and so far as I am concerned it is very difficult to decide. When you look at one set of figures it looks like there has been a serious falling off in the totals. Yet the minister and his staff have done their best to show that there has not been a falling off. But this misses the point I am coming to. On the question of recruiting there is no clear evidence.
The question of morale has been dealt with by men who have had experience in all branches of the services and they have emphasized that if we are going to have a defence force morale is the key to it. Canadians are a type of people much different from the British. We are certainly much different from the Americans. We tend to lack the discipline of the many centuries of military service which the English have. We tend to lack, do lack, and in fact are rather proud that we lack the statistical approach, the computer approach to manpower in our services that the Americans seem to have. We are different. I suggest that one cannot ignore the very sincere and heartfelt observations made by men in this house with much vaster military experience than I have, men who certainly climbed to higher ranks than I was able to achieve. They know the necessity of morale. I cannot deal with it. All I know is that the people do not know who has won the debate as to recruiting.
The second question which the layman is asking all across Canada is, will this bill save him, the taxpayer of Canada, money so that he can put that money into things desperately wanted by the Canadian people? I would say that in the beginning, eight months ago, the vast majority of laymen across the country were, like myself, in support of unification because they believed that it would save money. On the surface unification into one force instead of having three or more forces seemed to be the answer to a desperate need of our people.
The majority of our people do not object to the taxes which are necessary to maintain our military posture but they do wonder whether they are getting the maximum results for
National Defence Act Amendment their money when there are so many other things they want just as desperately. On this second issue, the saving of money, I have read the evidence on both sides and on the figures it looks like we are not saving money. The minister answers by saying that if we take the real value of money today we are saving or are roughly holding our own. But once again that is not clear to the public and so there is a certain amount of confusion.
In the last two or three days another issue has arisen, and this is the question of parliament itself. Ordinarily in our concept of government when we deal with a matter that requires expert advice we use the technique of the committee to draw from the experts answers to the questions which are in our minds.
The vast majority of the evidence given to the defence committee indicated that we should go slow, and take three to five years to decide on the question of unification. The military experts say, "Give us time to put integration into effect." I am assuming that we are all in favour of integration. If we believe in the parliamentary system we must consider the advice of these experts to the effect that we should take time on this very small item which is so close to the emotions and the hearts of the serving personnel, because to them matters such as the uniform and one service are desperately serious, something which I find it hard to understand. To a layman these are small points, but all the experts are asking is that the minister go slow.
Therefore I was very pleased today to detect what I thought was evidence of a trend toward moderation. We heard the minister say he would be willing to listen to proposals made on this side of the chamber for some sort of understanding over the week end. Therefore my next remarks are going to be directed toward some form of compromise proposal that will not only permit parliament to work effectively but will also move toward a more rational and responsible type of action.
Speaking now of the field in which I have some knowledge and dealing with the perspective of this bill and the over-all responsibilities of government, what do I see? First of all, military policy is not an end in itself. It is simply the operational arm of a policy of a government. The policies of the government in matters foreign and in matters economic must be clear to us in the house so that we may understand that in the bill which deals
April 14, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment with the operational arm, the military, designed to carry out one component part of government policies, there is coherence and there is logic.
At the present time and going back for many years Canada, not just under this government alone, has had no clearly delineated foreign policy. No government has directed its attention to what role this country, with 20 million people now and unlimited resources, is going to play in the future defence not only of this continent but in peacemaking all over the world and in space as well. We lack a clearly defined foreign policy which would enable us to know what type of military posture we must assume in order to carry out in our sphere of activity the foreign policy of our country.
o (2:40 p.m.)
To be more specific, how can parliament decide whether this bill is the correct and only course we should follow when we have had in the committee evidence to the effect that the unified force concept does not meet all the responsibilities which have been partially accepted by governments of the past and the present? For example, the United Nations is an organization which we have supported and still support. It was originally set up to include a United Nations force. That never came into being because of the veto power in the Security Council. In the last two or three years there have been proposals that smaller nations of some strength, which are not leaders in the major power struggle between the large nations, should have forces which could act in the policing role if the United Nations so requests. This is a concept which I believe members of all parties support. According to the evidence this type of unified force might be able to meet that function of a military posture.
Second, there is NATO. Is there any member of this house or any opinion leader in this country who does not know that the whole purpose and method of operation of NATO must be redefined? The need to redefine NATO both in the military and economic spheres has been clear for many years. The failure on the part of the members of NATO to define clearly for the next 10 or 15 years the purpose of NATO, in view of the new technology in the military field, makes it almost impossible for members of this house to make a learned and responsible decision in respect of this bill. We cannot do this until we know what our responsibilities in NATO will be.

The evidence given by the experts who appeared before the committee on national defence was that a unified force would not meet our present responsibilities to NATO. The fact that we do not have a 10 or 15 year projection of what our various responsibilities will be under NATO certainly adds weight to the view expressed by the experts that we should not rush into the unification concept and then take three to five years in bringing about a result which could be final and fatal.
Third, under NORAD we have responsibility under a treaty with the United States for the defence of the North American continent. Surely any person who has looked into the situation in respect of NORAD knows that this organization must be redefined in view of the new weapons which have come into technical use in the past few years. Once again we would be able to perform our function in this house in a much more responsible manner if we had a clearcut statement concerning the role of NORAD not only in the ballistic and antiballistic field but also in respect of the seacoast and the defence of North America.
The fourth point, which deeply concerns the members from the maritimes, is the question of the anti-submarine role allocated to Canada in the North Atlantic. Is this role to be discarded? We do not know. We are told it is still one of our responsibilities. Yet the experts tell us that under the unified force concept we cannot carry out this role. This is the type of evidence we have before us. Once again, instead of giving hints that we are going to withdraw and reduce our strength on the sea I think any responsible government, before asking us to rush into unification which could be so fateful, should give us a clearcut statement on this point.
Finally, and most important, is the matter of the defence of Canada itself. I believe there is a general hope that war never will come to the shores of the western continents of South and North America. However, I believe it is our responsibility to make plans to be able to defend our continent by land, by sea and by air. What is the capacity, what is the effectiveness of a unified force in Canada when working with a military force to the south and sharing the responsibility of carrying out this most vital of all the defence postures which have to be assumed in peacetime by Canada?
I believe the evidence here is most disturbing. It would seem to indicate that the
April 14, 1967

unification concept will not work in any modern concept of a joint defence of Canada which means, in truth, a joint defence of the continent. Therefore, since we do not know how this will be done under the unification concept, what is my proposal?
I suggested that I thought I had detected an air of moderation on both sides of the house earlier in the debate today. One idea which recommends itself to me is the proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. He put forward the simple proposal that we adjourn this debate and then bring the matter up again at the next session when a little more would be known about the plans of the defence department. I would like to modify this proposal, if I may, for a slightly different reason than was advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.
I believe there is general agreement in Canada that all the provisions of this bill must be debated with some responsibility by the members of this house. I suggest that a precedent has been set in this parliament during this session. We had before us a very difficult bill which was presented to this house last September concerning the national transportation commission. It had been introduced originally in 1964 and was so unacceptable that the government withdrew it. In 1966 they brought in a new bill on which they had worked for two years. It was a much better bill. Even though it was a much better bill, in the standing committee and in the committee of the whole house it was amended almost 80 times. On that occasion we had the Minister of Transport working with those of us in the opposition not only on the floor of the house but in the committee, outside the house, and in corridor sessions. Some of our amendments were accepted without debate and others were fought by the minister. Parliament then was at its best when members of all parties worked together to achieve, in respect of a matter which had tremendous implications for the transportation system of Canada, the best bill we could provide.
The key to the success in respect of that bill was the fact that the minister knew there were two or three items which were extremely controversial, just as we have two or three items in the 61 clauses of the bill we are now debating which are deeply controversial. For the sake of common sense and logic I would ask the minister to consider over the week end letting these two or three controversial clauses stand.
National Defence Act Amendment

I am not an authority on this bill but I would certainly suggest that clauses 2 and 6 should be put over. However,
I would ask that this matter be discussed with spokesmen on this side of the house because I am not an authority on the bill. I am sure the chairman of the defence committee will be glad to discuss it with the minister. If we could move into a consideration of other clauses of this bill in the way the people of this country expect I think we would clear up some of the controversial points that are bothering us. It is my hope that the minister will accept my main proposal in good faith. Several weeks ago we received a pleasant surprise. An article appeared on April 4 in the Toronto Globe and Mail headed "Hellyer Says Bill Statement Of Intent", "Instant Unification Is Ruled Out". In the body of the article the following is stated:
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Approval of the bill to unify the forces will not mean instant amalgamation of the navy, the army and the air force, Defence Minister Paul Hellyer assured the commons yesterday.
"It will be a statement of intention that the ultimate goal is a single service", he explained. "This must be known so that planning can proceed on an orderly basis."
I took from that statement there was an understanding in the minister's mind that it would take some time to implement this measure and therefore there would not be immediate unification. The minister confirms that understanding now by nodding his head.
Preceding that article another article appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on March 29 in respect of what the Prime Minister stated. This article states in part:
Prime Minister may exercise his influence to delay the implementation of the defence unification bill after it is passed.
Later in the article the following is stated:
-an effort on his part to see that defence minister Hellyer does not attempt to implement the unification legislation right away.
That article appeared about two and a half weeks ago and it gave a breath of hope that some statesmanship would emerge in this debate. I hope the minister will accept the suggestion that members on this side of the house are quite sincere in their concern about this matter and the people generally are concerned because they have yet to receive satisfactory answers.
We do not wish to hold up discussion on the clauses of this bill and I think we should

Which ones?
April 14, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment leave the controversial ones for later and consider the others. We should not ram the whole bill through at this time. The controversial clauses, perhaps 2, 6, and 61, which is the proclamation clause, should be deferred at this time and left to be dealt with at the next session. If the minister could bring back the drafted regulations at that time we would know what we were buying, know his plans in detail, and at that time we would be happier to deal with them.
It may be that the military experts are right that we should leave out one or two clauses of this bill and not deal with their purposes for a couple of years. However, if we knew the mechanics for unification we could then consider the body of the bill and move forward. In this way we could leave the controversial clauses until next session. In this way we could indicate to the country our desire to move forward on this bill but that we were not yet convinced of any immediate need for unification. The majority of the experts hold this view.
I am not an expert but I cannot see how a decision to put our forces into a single force and a single uniform would prevent integration. In this way I am sure we would show statesmanship on the part of this house and particularly on the part of the minister and the Prime Minister. This would be welcomed by the people of Canada and it would give the opposition a chance to show its willingness to co-operate.
Let me conclude by saying I think we are aiming at the wrong target in this debate when we aim at the minister. He has been somewhat inflexible, but I think the real target should be the lack of a foreign policy and a clear definition of what the government wishes the military to accomplish. Surely that is the root of the minister's difficulties. If he has been a little hard to get along with as an individual I suspect it is because he has been attempting to carry out an instruction he felt he was given. Now that we have received further information from the experts it would be wise on our part to put a little pressure on the Secretary of State for External Affairs to give us a clear definition on behalf of the government regarding the direction of our external affairs policy for the next 15 years. We could then define what we think our role in NATO and NORAD should be and what we should do about the anti-submarine role we are supposed to be playing. Certainly we have a right to know these things.

What are we going to do in respect of the defence of Canada and the continent? We should have a clearcut delineation in respect of this function. We might then be able to decide what to do about this bill. As I understand the evidence of the experts, a unified force will not help us meet our commitments to NATO and NORAD and certainly not to the defence of Canada. For that reason we have a right to ask the Prime Minister of our country to give that leadership prime ministers are expected to give at times of difficulties such as we are now experiencing.
My colleague, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, reminded us this morning of the defence production bill and that Mr. Howe had lost touch with reality in that it was introduced in peacetime in 1955 rather than in a time of war as in 1945. At that time Mr. St. Laurent watched the developments and realized that the house was approaching an impasse. He took the necessary and available steps, exercised the art of getting along, and asked Mr. Howe to disappear for a few days until arrangements with the opposition to accept an amended bill could be made. In other words, he properly exercised the functions of a Prime Minister.
If the minister has been forced to accept a rigid position, and we have seen this hurt him so far as public relations in this house and across the country are concerned, perhaps the Prime Minister could move in and accept the responsibility of making those little adjustments required to make possible the efficient working of this house. Canada would be well served if we had that type of statesmanship from the Prime Minister at this time.
I know enough about government policy to realize that the government cannot come out with policies in respect of NATO and NORAD overnight, but we could have some clear definition or indication of the direction in which we think our military should move. I hope the minister will consider this suggestion over the week end. After consultation between members on all sides perhaps we could deal with the non-controversial clauses of the bill and then come to some conclusion about what to do with the controversial clauses in light of what the experts have said.
